claim: Gamma oscillations in visual cortex have been hypothesized to be critical for perception, cognition, and information transfer.
source: Gamma oscillations in visual cortex have been hypothesized to be critical for perception, cognition, and information transfer.
evidence: This is a statement about existing hypotheses in the field, supported by the general scientific literature on gamma oscillations.

claim: Observations of gamma oscillations in visual cortex vary widely across studies.
source: However, observations of these oscillations in visual cortex vary widely; some studies report little to no stimulus-induced narrowband gamma oscillations, others report oscillations for only some stimuli, and yet others report large oscillations for most stimuli.
evidence: This statement summarizes the variability in findings across different studies in the literature.

claim: The authors developed a model that predicts gamma responses for arbitrary images.
source: To better understand this signal, we developed a model that predicts gamma responses for arbitrary images and validated this model on electrocorticography (ECoG) data from human visual cortex.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the study's main contribution.

claim: The model computes variance across the outputs of spatially pooled orientation channels.
source: The model computes variance across the outputs of spatially pooled orientation channels, and accurately predicts gamma amplitude across 86 images.
evidence: This describes the computational approach of the model developed in the study.

claim: The model accurately predicts gamma amplitude across 86 images.
source: The model computes variance across the outputs of spatially pooled orientation channels, and accurately predicts gamma amplitude across 86 images.
evidence: This is a claim about the model's performance, supported by the experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Gamma responses were large for a small subset of stimuli.
source: Gamma responses were large for a small subset of stimuli, differing dramatically from fMRI and ECoG broadband (non-oscillatory) responses.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings showing sparse gamma responses.

claim: Gamma responses differ dramatically from fMRI and ECoG broadband responses.
source: Gamma responses were large for a small subset of stimuli, differing dramatically from fMRI and ECoG broadband (non-oscillatory) responses.
evidence: This comparison is supported by the data presented in the manuscript showing different response patterns.

claim: Gamma oscillations in visual cortex serve as a biomarker of gain control rather than being a fundamental mechanism for communicating visual information.
source: We propose that gamma oscillations in visual cortex serve as a biomarker of gain control rather than being a fundamental mechanism for communicating visual information.
evidence: This is the main interpretive conclusion of the study, based on the pattern of results and their relationship to gain control mechanisms.

claim: Image-computable models have been developed for fMRI BOLD signal.
source: Image-computable models, which predict responses to arbitrary, unlabeled images, have been developed for the functional MRI (fMRI) blood oxygen level dependent (BOLD) signal (Dumoulin and Wandell, 2008; Güçlü and van Gerven, 2015; Kay et al., 2013b; Kay et al., 2013a) and for spiking of single neurons in animals (Mante et al., 2008; Rust et al., 2005; Simoncelli and Heeger, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work in the field.

claim: Image-computable models have been developed for spiking of single neurons in animals.
source: Image-computable models, which predict responses to arbitrary, unlabeled images, have been developed for the functional MRI (fMRI) blood oxygen level dependent (BOLD) signal (Dumoulin and Wandell, 2008; Güçlü and van Gerven, 2015; Kay et al., 2013b; Kay et al., 2013a) and for spiking of single neurons in animals (Mante et al., 2008; Rust et al., 2005; Simoncelli and Heeger, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work in the field.

claim: There are no image-computable models to predict oscillations in the gamma band of the local field potential.
source: In contrast, to our knowledge, there are no image-computable models to predict oscillations in the gamma band (30–80 Hz) of the local field potential (but see Discussion), although gamma oscillations have been intensely studied and are a prominent part of many neural recordings and theories of neural function (Jensen et al., 2007; Tallon-Baudry and Bertrand, 1999).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field prior to this work.

claim: Oriented bars elicit large gamma responses in visual cortex.
source: In particular, oriented bars (Gray and Singer, 1989; Gray et al., 1989) and gratings (Eckhorn et al., 1988; Hermes et al., 2017a; Muthukumaraswamy and Singh, 2008) elicit large gamma responses in visual cortex.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior experimental work.

claim: Gratings elicit large gamma responses in visual cortex.
source: In particular, oriented bars (Gray and Singer, 1989; Gray et al., 1989) and gratings (Eckhorn et al., 1988; Hermes et al., 2017a; Muthukumaraswamy and Singh, 2008) elicit large gamma responses in visual cortex.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior experimental work.

claim: Gamma responses tend to increase with stimulus size.
source: The responses tend to increase with stimulus size and contrast (Gieselmann and Thiele, 2008; Henrie and Shapley, 2005; Ray and Maunsell, 2011), and tend to decrease in the presence of unstructured noise (Bartoli et al., 2019; Hermes et al., 2015; Jia et al., 2013; Kayser et al., 2003) or multiple orientations (Bartolo et al., 2011; Lima et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior experimental work.

claim: Gamma responses tend to increase with stimulus contrast.
source: The responses tend to increase with stimulus size and contrast (Gieselmann and Thiele, 2008; Henrie and Shapley, 2005; Ray and Maunsell, 2011), and tend to decrease in the presence of unstructured noise (Bartoli et al., 2019; Hermes et al., 2015; Jia et al., 2013; Kayser et al., 2003) or multiple orientations (Bartolo et al., 2011; Lima et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior experimental work.

claim: Gamma responses tend to decrease in the presence of unstructured noise.
source: The responses tend to increase with stimulus size and contrast (Gieselmann and Thiele, 2008; Henrie and Shapley, 2005; Ray and Maunsell, 2011), and tend to decrease in the presence of unstructured noise (Bartoli et al., 2019; Hermes et al., 2015; Jia et al., 2013; Kayser et al., 2003) or multiple orientations (Bartolo et al., 2011; Lima et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior experimental work.

claim: Gamma responses tend to decrease in the presence of multiple orientations.
source: The responses tend to increase with stimulus size and contrast (Gieselmann and Thiele, 2008; Henrie and Shapley, 2005; Ray and Maunsell, 2011), and tend to decrease in the presence of unstructured noise (Bartoli et al., 2019; Hermes et al., 2015; Jia et al., 2013; Kayser et al., 2003) or multiple orientations (Bartolo et al., 2011; Lima et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior experimental work.

claim: Some images of scenes and objects cause large reliable gamma oscillations while others do not.
source: Some images of scenes and objects cause large reliable gamma oscillations while others do not (Brunet et al., 2015; Hermes et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior experimental work.

claim: Gamma response selectivity differs from that of the BOLD response.
source: Gamma response selectivity differs from that of the BOLD response (Hermes et al., 2017b; Muthukumaraswamy and Singh, 2009) and single- and multi-unit spike rates (Jia et al., 2013; Peter et al., 2019; Ray and Maunsell, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior experimental work.

claim: Gamma response selectivity differs from single- and multi-unit spike rates.
source: Gamma response selectivity differs from that of the BOLD response (Hermes et al., 2017b; Muthukumaraswamy and Singh, 2009) and single- and multi-unit spike rates (Jia et al., 2013; Peter et al., 2019; Ray and Maunsell, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior experimental work.

claim: Increasing grating size causes gamma oscillations to increase in power while causing firing rates to decrease in primary visual cortex.
source: For example, when recording from the same electrode in primary visual cortex (V1), increasing grating size causes gamma oscillations to increase in power while causing firing rates to decrease (Jia et al., 2013; Ray and Maunsell, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior experimental work.

claim: Gamma power decreases dramatically with noise masking while population firing rates do not change substantially.
source: Gamma power also decreases dramatically with noise masking while population firing rates do not change substantially (Jia et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior experimental work.

claim: The authors measured responses from ECoG electrodes over visual cortex while human subjects viewed a variety of different images.
source: Here, we measured responses from electrocorticography (ECoG) electrodes over visual cortex while human subjects viewed a variety of different images.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: The ECoG response was separated into broadband and narrowband gamma components.
source: We separated the ECoG response into two spectrally overlapping components: one broadband (spanning 30–200 Hz) and one narrowband (centered between 30–80 Hz).
evidence: This describes the signal processing approach used in the study.

claim: The broadband response was well fit by a model adapted from fMRI of visual cortex.
source: The broadband response was well fit by a model adapted from fMRI of visual cortex (Kay et al., 2013b).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by the modeling results presented.

claim: The narrowband gamma responses were strikingly different from broadband responses.
source: The narrowband gamma responses were strikingly different, and we developed a new, image-computable model in order to explain those responses.
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by the data presented.

claim: The differences in response patterns and models suggest that broadband signals and narrowband gamma originate from distinct aspects of neural circuitry.
source: The differences in the patterns of responses and the differences in the two models suggest that broadband signals and narrowband gamma originate from distinct aspects of neural circuitry.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion based on the differences observed in the study.

claim: Six electrodes were identified in the first subject, two in the second subject, and seven in the third subject.
source: This yielded six electrodes in the first subject, two in the second subject and seven in the third subject (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental sample, shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Power spectra were separated into oscillatory and non-oscillatory components by modeling the log-power/log-frequency spectrum as the sum of 3 components: a linear baseline, a constant, and a Gaussian centered between 30 and 80 Hz.
source: As in previous work (Hermes et al., 2015), we separated the power spectra into an oscillatory and non-oscillatory component by modeling the log-power/log-frequency spectrum as the sum of 3 components: a linear baseline, a constant, and a Gaussian centered between 30 and 80 Hz (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the analytical method used, with reference to prior work and illustration in Figure 1B.

claim: The narrowband gamma and the broadband signal overlap in frequency content and are distinguished by the pattern in the spectral data.
source: In our quantification, the narrowband gamma and the broadband signal overlap in frequency content, and are distinguished by the pattern in the spectral data.
evidence: This explains the analytical approach used to separate the two signal types.

claim: The two components (narrowband gamma and broadband) do not depend on one another.
source: Despite the overlap, the two components do not depend on one another: it is possible to obtain a positive broadband component with zero narrowband gamma, zero broadband component with positive narrowband gamma, or a mixture of the two types of components.
evidence: This is an explanation of the independence of the two signal components based on the modeling approach.

claim: Large increases in narrowband gamma power are observed for large, high-contrast grating patterns but not for noise patterns.
source: Replicating previous results (Hermes et al., 2015; Jia et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2008), we observe large increases in narrowband gamma power for large, high-contrast grating patterns but not for noise patterns, and strong broadband responses for both grating patterns and noise stimuli (Figure 1B–C).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, shown in Figure 1B-C and consistent with prior work.

claim: Strong broadband responses are observed for both grating patterns and noise stimuli.
source: Replicating previous results (Hermes et al., 2015; Jia et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2008), we observe large increases in narrowband gamma power for large, high-contrast grating patterns but not for noise patterns, and strong broadband responses for both grating patterns and noise stimuli (Figure 1B–C).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, shown in Figure 1B-C.

claim: Stimulus selectivity is similar for broadband ECoG and BOLD but quite different for gamma oscillations.
source: We find that stimulus selectivity is similar for broadband ECoG and BOLD but quite different for gamma oscillations.
evidence: This is a summary finding from the study comparing the three signal types.

claim: BOLD responses in the example voxel are generally similar to broadband ECoG data.
source: The pattern of responses in the BOLD data is generally similar to that of the broadband ECoG data (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a comparison shown in Figure 2, based on data from the current study and prior work.

claim: ECoG narrowband gamma responses are quite different from BOLD and broadband responses.
source: In contrast, the ECoG narrowband gamma responses (Figure 2D) are quite different.
evidence: This is a finding from the study, illustrated in Figure 2D.

claim: BOLD signal and ECoG broadband power are largest for patterns with multiple orientations.
source: The BOLD signal and ECoG broadband power are largest for patterns with multiple orientations, such as the curvy patterns in images 74-78 (and similar patterns from the ∆space stimuli that overlapped the pRFs, including images 8-16 and 30-36).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on the data presented.

claim: The biggest gamma response is to high-contrast gratings.
source: The opposite is true for the gamma responses, for which the biggest response by far is to high-contrast gratings, and for which no significant responses were found for space stimuli (relative to the response to blank stimuli, based on bootstrapping across trials; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on the data presented.

claim: No significant gamma responses were found for space stimuli relative to blank stimuli.
source: The opposite is true for the gamma responses, for which the biggest response by far is to high-contrast gratings, and for which no significant responses were found for space stimuli (relative to the response to blank stimuli, based on bootstrapping across trials; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on statistical testing.

claim: For all three signal types, responses increased with stimulus contrast for a given pattern.
source: For all three signal types, if there is a response to a stimulus of a particular pattern, such as gratings (images 47-50) or plaids (images 51-54), then responses increased with stimulus contrast for that pattern.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on the data presented.

claim: Broadband responses to curved patterns are high whereas gamma responses are relatively low compared to grating responses.
source: In particular the broadband responses to curved patterns (stimuli 1–39) are high whereas the gamma responses are relatively low compared to the grating responses.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on the averaged data across electrodes.

claim: Broadband increases with the number of component gratings, whereas narrowband gamma decreases with the number of component gratings.
source: Another systematic difference between the two types of responses is that broadband increases with the number of component gratings, whereas narrowband gamma decreases with the number of component gratings (Figure 2E insets, showing the responses to stimuli made from 1 (grating), 2 (plaid), or 16 (circular) component gratings).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, illustrated in Figure 2E insets.

claim: ECoG broadband responses typically correlate well with BOLD in visual cortex.
source: Since ECoG broadband responses typically correlate well with BOLD in visual cortex (Hermes et al., 2017b; Winawer et al., 2013), we tested whether a second-order contrast model (SOC) developed for fMRI could accurately fit, and predict, the ECoG broadband signal (Kay et al., 2013b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The SOC model is a two-stage LNN (Linear-Nonlinear-Nonlinear) cascade model.
source: The SOC model is a two-stage LNN (Linear-Nonlinear-Nonlinear) cascade model.
evidence: This describes the structure of the SOC model.

claim: The SOC model explained an average of 80% of the cross-validated variance across the 15 ECoG electrodes.
source: Although there are some discrepancies (especially in stimuli 79–86), the model fit the data well overall and explained an average of 80% (coefficient of determination) of the cross-validated variance across the 15 ECoG electrodes.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the modeling analysis.

claim: The OV model computes variance across the outputs of spatially pooled orientation channels within a pRF.
source: We propose a new model, called the Orientation Variance (OV) model, that computes variance across the outputs of spatially pooled orientation channels within a pRF.
evidence: This describes the computational approach of the OV model.

claim: The OV model builds on known computations in the visual cortex.
source: Similar to the SOC model, the OV model builds on known computations in the visual cortex, but differs in the way signals are pooled across orientation bands (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a statement about the biological plausibility of the model, illustrated in Figure 4.

claim: Long-range horizontal connections in visual cortex preferentially connect cortical columns tuned to the same orientation.
source: This computation can be thought of as an analog to the long-range horizontal connections in visual cortex, which preferentially connect cortical columns tuned to the same orientation (Gilbert and Wiesel, 1983; Hata et al., 1988).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior neuroanatomical work.

claim: The OV model predicts a large response when variance across orientations is high and a small response when variance is low.
source: The OV model predicts a large response when variance across orientations is high and a small response when variance is low.
evidence: This describes the key property of the OV model.

claim: The OV model output increases with contrast within the pRF.
source: The OV model thus has two important properties: first, the output increases with contrast within the pRF (high contrast gratings produce higher responses than low contrast gratings), and second, the output increases with increasing variance across orientated contrast energy within the pRF (gratings produce higher responses than plaids, and plaids produce higher responses than curved patterns, consistent with the observed data in Figure 2E, insets).
evidence: This describes a property of the OV model, consistent with the data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The OV model output increases with increasing variance across oriented contrast energy within the pRF.
source: The OV model thus has two important properties: first, the output increases with contrast within the pRF (high contrast gratings produce higher responses than low contrast gratings), and second, the output increases with increasing variance across orientated contrast energy within the pRF (gratings produce higher responses than plaids, and plaids produce higher responses than curved patterns, consistent with the observed data in Figure 2E, insets).
evidence: This describes a property of the OV model, consistent with the data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The OV model accounted for an average of 75% cross-validated variance explained across electrodes.
source: Overall, the OV model accounted for the pattern of gamma responses well, with an average of 75% cross-validated variance explained across electrodes.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the modeling analysis.

claim: The OV model has five parameters: the location and size of the pRF (x, y and σ), a gain factor (g) and an exponent (n).
source: The OV model has five parameters: the location and size of the pRF (x, y and σ), a gain factor (g) and an exponent (n).
evidence: This describes the parameters of the OV model.

claim: The pRF center and size could not be robustly obtained by fitting a model to the gamma responses across the 86 images.
source: The pRF center and size were derived from separate data, as they could not be robustly obtained by fitting a model to the gamma responses across the 86 images.
evidence: This explains a methodological choice in the modeling approach.

claim: Stimuli that varied systematically in spatial position induced very little gamma response.
source: This is because the stimuli that varied systematically in spatial position (images 1 to 38) induced very little gamma response.
evidence: This is a finding from the study explaining why pRF parameters couldn't be fit from gamma responses.

claim: The x and y position of the population receptive field were fixed based on the SOC fits to the broadband data.
source: We fixed the x and y position of the population receptive field based on the SOC fits to the broadband data (Figure 3).
evidence: This describes a methodological choice in the modeling approach.

claim: Across electrodes an exponent of n = 0.5 predicted most variance in the left-out data.
source: Across electrodes an exponent of n = 0.5 predicted most variance in the left-out data, and results with this exponent are reported throughout this paper.
evidence: This is a finding from the model optimization procedure.

claim: The OV model explained significantly more variance in the gamma responses (75%) compared to the SOC model (62%).
source: The OV model explained significantly more variance in the gamma responses (75%) compared to the SOC model (62%) (p<0.005 by a paired t-test on Fisher transform of the R2), see Figure 7 (red) and Table 1.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the model comparison, shown in Figure 7 and Table 1.

claim: The OV model explained significantly more variance in the gamma responses compared to a mean model (26%).
source: The OV model also explained significantly more variance in the gamma responses compared to a mean model, which predicts the same response level to all stimuli (26%, p<0.001, see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the model comparison.

claim: The SOC model explained significantly more variance in the broadband responses (80%) compared to the OV model (24%).
source: Conversely, the SOC model explained significantly more variance in the broadband responses (80%) compared to the OV model (24%) (p<0.001), see Figure 7 (blue) and Table 1.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the model comparison, shown in Figure 7 and Table 1.

claim: The SOC model explained significantly more variance in the broadband responses compared to a mean model (41%).
source: The SOC model also explained significantly more variance in the broadband responses compared to a mean model (41%) (p<0.001).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the model comparison.

claim: The model comparisons suggest that fundamentally different computations underlie broadband and gamma responses.
source: The model comparisons we have performed suggest that fundamentally different computations underlie broadband and gamma responses.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion based on the modeling results.

claim: The OV model is sensitive to the distribution of contrast energy across orientations within the pRF, but not to image structure remote from the pRF.
source: The OV model is sensitive to the distribution of contrast energy across orientations within the pRF, but not to image structure remote from the pRF.
evidence: This describes a property of the OV model.

claim: It is critical to consider the precise receptive field location of an electrode when investigating gamma oscillations.
source: This example illustrates that it is critical to consider the precise receptive field location of an electrode when investigating gamma oscillations.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the examples shown in Figure 8.

claim: The OV outputs for natural images are, in general, strikingly low compared to high-contrast gratings.
source: High-contrast gratings are often used in studies of gamma oscillations, for example (Eckhorn et al., 1988; Hoogenboom et al., 2006; Rohenkohl et al., 2018); using these stimuli as a benchmark, we find that the OV outputs for natural images are, in general, strikingly low.
evidence: This is a finding from the natural image simulations, with citations to prior work using gratings.

claim: Natural images occasionally have oriented high-contrast energy within the pRF and these give rise to large OV output.
source: However, natural images occasionally have oriented high-contrast energy within the pRF and these give rise to large OV output (Figure 9).
evidence: This is a finding from the natural image simulations, shown in Figure 9.

claim: For most natural gray-scale images, relatively low levels of gamma oscillations are expected.
source: To the degree that the OV model accurately predicts narrowband gamma responses and the SOC model accurately predicts broadband responses, these results indicate that for most natural gray-scale images (with occasional exceptions), relatively low levels of gamma oscillations are expected.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the natural image simulations.

claim: The narrowband gamma responses were much sparser than the broadband responses.
source: The most salient observation is that the narrowband gamma responses were much sparser than the broadband responses.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding from the study.

claim: The gamma responses were large for only a few stimuli tested (high contrast gratings), and relatively small or even within the experimental noise for most other stimuli.
source: The gamma responses were large for only a few stimuli tested (high contrast gratings), and relatively small or even within the experimental noise for most other stimuli (e.g., noise patterns and textures with a lot of curvature).
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding from the study.

claim: The sparseness in the narrowband gamma responses was not due to a lack of image contrast or measurement sensitivity.
source: The sparseness in the narrowband gamma responses was not due to a lack of image contrast or measurement sensitivity.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings, ruling out alternative explanations.

claim: Large broadband responses were observed for most stimuli tested, including all stimuli with high contrast within the electrode's receptive field.
source: In fact, large broadband responses were observed for most stimuli tested, including all stimuli with high contrast within the electrode's receptive field (pRF).
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: The much greater sparseness in the narrowband gamma compared to broadband responses was observed in every electrode studied.
source: The much greater sparseness in the narrowband gamma compared to broadband responses was a highly consistent finding, observed in every electrode studied (n = 15, coming from three subjects and spanning V1-V3).
evidence: This is a summary of the consistency of the findings across the sample.

claim: The fMRI response was large for all stimuli with high contrast in the pRF and tended to be larger for curved patterns than for gratings.
source: Like broadband, the fMRI response was large for all stimuli with high contrast in the pRF and tended to be larger for curved patterns than for gratings.
evidence: This is a finding from the comparison with prior fMRI data.

claim: The similarity in stimulus selectivity between fMRI and broadband is consistent with a number of other studies indicating good agreement between the two types of signals.
source: The similarity in stimulus selectivity between fMRI and broadband is consistent with a number of other studies indicating good agreement between the two types of signals.
evidence: This is supported by the subsequent citations to prior work.

claim: Conclusions about gamma oscillations in human visual cortex cannot be directly transferred to other systems without careful testing.
source: Conclusions about gamma oscillations in human visual cortex can thus not be directly transferred to other systems without careful testing.
evidence: This is a cautionary statement about the generalizability of the findings.

claim: Both SOC and OV models predict that response amplitudes should increase with stimulus contrast.
source: The two models share a common first stage, in which contrast energy is computed. As a result, both models predict that response amplitudes should increase with stimulus contrast, in agreement with the observation that fMRI, broadband, and narrowband ECoG responses all increase with contrast.
evidence: This is a description of a shared property of the two models, consistent with the data.

claim: The SOC model first sums across orientation at each spatial location and then computes variance across space.
source: The SOC model first sums across orientation at each spatial location and then computes variance across space.
evidence: This describes the computational approach of the SOC model.

claim: The OV model first sums across space (within each orientation band) and then computes variance across orientations.
source: The OV model does the opposite, first summing across space (within each orientation band) and then computing variance across orientations.
evidence: This describes the computational approach of the OV model.

claim: The SOC model is blind to the variance in orientations within the population receptive field.
source: The SOC model is blind to the variance in orientations within the population receptive field and the OV model is blind to the variance in contrast energy across space within the population receptive field.
evidence: This describes a property of the SOC model.

claim: The OV model is blind to the variance in contrast energy across space within the population receptive field.
source: The SOC model is blind to the variance in orientations within the population receptive field and the OV model is blind to the variance in contrast energy across space within the population receptive field.
evidence: This describes a property of the OV model.

claim: The SOC model penalizes images (lowers the response) when contrast is high everywhere, akin to surround suppression.
source: Also, the SOC model penalizes images (lowers the response) when contrast is high everywhere, akin to surround suppression.
evidence: This describes a property of the SOC model.

claim: The OV model responses grow with stimulus size, as is observed for gamma oscillations but not spiking or BOLD.
source: Because the OV model first sums across space, responses grow with stimulus size, as is observed for gamma oscillations but not spiking (Gieselmann and Thiele, 2008; Jia et al., 2013; Ray and Maunsell, 2011; Self et al., 2016) or BOLD (Press et al., 2001; Zenger-Landolt and Heeger, 2003; Zuiderbaan et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes a property of the OV model, consistent with prior findings cited.

claim: Color has been shown to strongly modulate gamma.
source: For example, color has recently been shown to strongly modulate gamma (Peter et al., 2019; Shirhatti and Ray, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent work.

claim: Image contrast (first order contrast) and variations in contrast (second order contrast) are not sufficient to elicit robust gamma oscillations.
source: Using well controlled stimuli, our data show that image contrast (first order contrast) and variations in contrast (second order contrast) are, in and of themselves, not sufficient to elicit robust gamma oscillations.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study based on the experimental findings.

claim: Another group independently tested models of gamma oscillations in visual cortex using images of complex objects and scenes, reaching opposite conclusions.
source: While the OV model was in development, another group independently tested models of gamma oscillations in visual cortex using images of complex objects and scenes, reaching opposite conclusions (Brunet and Fries, 2019).
evidence: This is a reference to concurrent work in the field.

claim: Inferring the stimulus properties that drive neural responses from studies using natural images is difficult because of unmodeled correlations that are widespread in natural images.
source: Inferring the stimulus properties that drive neural responses from such studies is difficult because of unmodeled correlations that are widespread in natural images (Rust and Movshon, 2005).
evidence: This is a methodological point supported by a citation.

claim: The advantage of carefully controlled stimulus properties is that the interpretation of the results is more straightforward.
source: The advantage of carefully controlled stimulus properties is that the interpretation of the results is more straightforward, as is the link between the computations in the model and the pattern of responses.
evidence: This is a methodological justification for the experimental approach.

claim: The method of separating the ECoG measurement into two components was important for revealing the sparseness of gamma responses.
source: The method of separating the ECoG measurement into two components was also important. Had we simply characterized the gamma response as the band-limited power increase over baseline, the gamma responses would have appeared less sparse.
evidence: This is a methodological point about the importance of the analytical approach.

claim: Studies that do not explicitly separate broadband and narrowband gamma oscillations might draw conclusions about the function of narrowband oscillations when the signals measured could reflect broadband responses.
source: Studies that do not explicitly separate broadband and narrowband gamma oscillations might draw conclusions about the function of narrowband oscillations when the signals measured could, in fact, reflect broadband responses.
evidence: This is a cautionary statement about the interpretation of gamma oscillations in other studies.

claim: Percent signal change in gamma responses is much larger than that for broadband responses.
source: We observed that percent signal change in gamma responses is much larger than that for broadband responses.
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: Broadband responses are thought to arise from asynchronous neural activity.
source: Broadband responses are thought to arise from asynchronous neural activity (Miller et al., 2009b), which results in substantial cancellation in the pooled field potential (Butler et al., 2017; Hermes et al., 2017b; Krusienski et al., 2011; Winawer et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Narrowband gamma responses are thought to reflect synchronous activity across a neuronal population.
source: Narrowband gamma responses, in contrast, are thought to reflect synchronous activity across a neuronal population (Hasenstaub et al., 2005; Jia et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The synchronous response can result in a much larger macroscopic field potential even if it comes from a much smaller neuronal population.
source: The synchronous response, even if it comes from a much smaller neuronal population, can result in a much larger macroscopic field potential (Butler et al., 2017; Hermes et al., 2017b; Winawer et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The large size of the field potential generated by gamma oscillations does not imply a high level of neuronal population activity in terms of energy demand or spike rates.
source: Hence the large size of the field potential generated by gamma oscillations does not imply a high level of neuronal population activity in terms of energy demand or spike rates.
evidence: This is an inference based on the understanding of how field potentials are generated.

claim: A large neuronal response can occur in the absence of gamma oscillations.
source: Similarly, a large neuronal response can occur in the absence of gamma oscillations.
evidence: This is supported by the example that follows in the text.

claim: Multiunit recordings in macaque V1 and MT to sweeping bars showed oscillating responses in only 2 of 424 recordings, while noting increases in firing rates and broadband LFP.
source: For example, multiunit recordings in macaque V1 and MT to sweeping bars showed oscillating responses in only 2 of 424 recordings, while noting increases in firing rates and broadband LFP (Young et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Substantial increases in broadband power generally correlate with both high energy consumption and high firing rates.
source: In contrast, substantial increases in broadband power generally correlate with both high energy consumption (Hermes et al., 2017b; Winawer et al., 2013) and high firing rates (Manning et al., 2009; Ojemann et al., 2013; Ray and Maunsell, 2011) (though for an exception see [Leszczynski et al., 2019]).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work, with a noted exception.

claim: The highly specific stimulus selectivity of narrowband gamma raises questions about the potential functions of this signal.
source: The highly specific stimulus selectivity of narrowband gamma raises questions about the potential functions of this signal.
evidence: This is an interpretive statement based on the findings.

claim: A wide range of cognitive and neural functions have been attributed to gamma oscillations, including perceptual binding of visual features, prioritizing communication of certain visual information, and visual awareness.
source: A wide range of cognitive and neural functions have been attributed to gamma oscillations, including perceptual binding of visual features (Eckhorn et al., 1988; Gray et al., 1989), prioritizing communication of certain visual information over other information (Fries, 2005), and visual awareness (Engel and Singer, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior theoretical work.

claim: If gamma oscillations are a leading cause of visual awareness or feedforward visual communication, then the oscillations should be observed for any clearly visible stimulus.
source: However, it is reasonable to expect that if gamma oscillations are a leading cause of visual awareness, or of feedforward visual communication, then the oscillations should be observed for any clearly visible stimulus.
evidence: This is a logical inference about what would be expected if certain theories were correct.

claim: Stimuli such as circular patterns elicit robust signals in visual cortex as measured with fMRI and broadband ECoG.
source: At high contrast, all of these stimuli are easily visible and all of them elicit robust signals in visual cortex as measured with fMRI and broadband ECoG.
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: Stimuli such as circular patterns would be expected to elicit strong multiunit responses, given typical models of action potentials in neuronal populations in primary visual cortex.
source: Moreover, these stimuli would be expected to elicit strong multiunit responses, given typical models of action potentials in neuronal populations in primary visual cortex (e.g., [Carandini et al., 2005; Rust et al., 2005]).
evidence: This is an inference based on prior models, supported by citations.

claim: Stimuli such as circular patterns evoke large and reliable BOLD signals in higher visual areas such as hV4.
source: In fact, fMRI studies show that stimuli such as circular patterns, which elicit no detectable narrowband gamma signal beyond baseline signal levels, do evoke large and reliable BOLD signals in higher visual areas such as hV4 (Kay et al., 2013b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Visual signals are transmitted along the visual hierarchy for stimulus features to which no reliable narrowband gamma signals are measured in the corresponding retinotopic locations of V1.
source: Hence visual signals are transmitted along the visual hierarchy for stimulus features to which we measure no reliable narrowband gamma signals in the corresponding retinotopic locations of V1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the fMRI findings in higher visual areas.

claim: It is unlikely for gamma oscillations to be the primary means of communicating long-range feedforward visual information.
source: This suggests that it is unlikely for gamma oscillations to be the primary means of communicating long-range feedforward visual information.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings.

claim: Theories proposing a role for gamma oscillations are pitched at a general level and do not make quantitative predictions about the amplitude of the oscillations for specific stimuli or conditions.
source: One is that theories proposing a role for gamma oscillations are pitched at a general level and do not make quantitative predictions about the amplitude of the oscillations for specific stimuli or conditions.
evidence: This is a critique of existing theories.

claim: It is possible that very small oscillations exist and serve critical functions.
source: Secondly, we acknowledge that there may be small oscillations that are not detectable using our current measurement methods. It is therefore possible that very small oscillations exist and serve critical functions.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation of the study.

claim: Large oscillations are likely to influence spiking excitability or information transfer.
source: Large oscillations are likely to influence spiking excitability (Jensen et al., 2007) or information transfer (Besserve et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Large-amplitude gamma oscillations are found for stimuli that are high in contrast, spatially extended, and with few orientations.
source: Both in this report and elsewhere (Gieselmann and Thiele, 2008; Henrie and Shapley, 2005; Jia et al., 2013; Ray and Maunsell, 2011), large-amplitude gamma oscillations are found for stimuli that are high in contrast, spatially extended, and with few orientations.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from this study and prior work.

claim: High contrast, spatial extent, and limited orientations all produce larger outputs in the OV model and are all associated with gain control or suppression in neuronal circuits.
source: These three image properties—contrast, spatial extent, and limited orientations—all produce larger outputs in the OV model, and interestingly, are all associated with gain control or suppression in neuronal circuits.
evidence: This is an observation linking the model properties to known neural mechanisms.

claim: Stimulus contrast has been linked to inhibition in divisive normalization models of primary visual cortex.
source: First, stimulus contrast has been linked to inhibition in divisive normalization models of primary visual cortex (Heeger, 1992).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior modeling work.

claim: Gain control increases with local stimulus contrast, possibly via shunting inhibition or a reduction in recurrent amplification.
source: According to this model, gain control increases with local stimulus contrast, possibly via shunting inhibition (an increase in membrane conductance) or a reduction in recurrent amplification (Sato et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Neuronal responses such as spike rates tend to increase with contrast, but the rate of increase is slower at higher contrast, consistent with mechanisms of increasing gain control at higher contrast.
source: Although neuronal responses such as spike rates tend to increase with contrast, the rate of increase is slower at higher contrast (Albrecht and Hamilton, 1982), consistent with mechanisms of increasing gain control at higher contrast (Albrecht and Geisler, 1991; Heeger, 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Stimulus extent is linked to suppression in that larger stimuli stimulate the inhibitory surrounds of neuronal receptive fields, thereby reducing the neuronal response.
source: Second, stimulus extent is linked to suppression in that larger stimuli stimulate the inhibitory surrounds of neuronal receptive fields, thereby reducing the neuronal response (Allman et al., 1985).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: For a large stimulus, surround suppression is more effective when an annulus and a central stimulus match in orientation.
source: Third, for a large stimulus, surround suppression is more effective when an annulus and a central stimulus match in orientation (Cavanaugh et al., 2002; DeAngelis et al., 1994; Knierim and van Essen, 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Each of the three stimulus properties (high contrast, large spatial extent, limited orientations) is associated with more gain control or suppression as well as a larger OV output, consistent with the interpretation that gamma oscillations are a biomarker of gain control or normalization.
source: In summary, each of these three stimulus properties (high contrast, large spatial extent, limited orientations) is associated with more gain control or suppression as well as a larger OV output, consistent with the interpretation that gamma oscillations are a biomarker of gain control or normalization, an idea previously proposed based on physiology data from macaque visual cortex (Ray et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion linking the findings to a prior proposal, supported by a citation.

claim: Ray et al. (2013) showed that stimulus manipulations thought to increase normalization lead to larger amplitude gamma oscillations.
source: Ray et al., (2013) showed that stimulus manipulations thought to increase normalization lead to larger amplitude gamma oscillations.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from prior work.

claim: When a null-motion stimulus is added to a preferred motion stimulus, spike rates decrease and gamma oscillations increase in amplitude.
source: For example, when a null-motion stimulus is added to a preferred motion stimulus, spike rates decrease, indicating an inhibitory effect of the null motion stimulus, and gamma oscillations increase in amplitude (Ray et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from prior work.

claim: The link between gamma oscillations and gain control does not necessarily indicate what causal role, if any, the oscillations have in neural processing.
source: We note that the link between gamma oscillations and gain control does not necessarily indicate what causal role, if any, the oscillations have in neural processing.
evidence: This is a cautionary statement about the interpretation of the findings.

claim: At a minimum, the oscillations may serve as a biomarker of gain control circuits, useful to the experimenter but not necessarily to the organism producing them.
source: At a minimum, the oscillations may serve as a biomarker of gain control circuits, useful to the experimenter but not necessarily to the organism producing them.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Increasing the number of superimposed gratings decreases the OV output and the power of narrowband gamma, yet causes an increase in cross-orientation suppression in visual cortex.
source: One exception to the link between inhibition and gamma power in this study is the effect of the number of component orientations: increasing the number of superimposed gratings decreases the OV output and the power of narrowband gamma (Figure 3), yet causes an increase in cross-orientation suppression in visual cortex (Bonds, 1989; Morrone et al., 1982).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, with citations to prior work on cross-orientation suppression.

claim: Cross-orientation suppression and surround suppression differ in several ways, including in their temporal properties, with surround suppression slightly delayed.
source: Cross-orientation suppression and surround suppression differ in several ways, including in their temporal properties, with surround suppression slightly delayed (Smith et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Cross-orientation suppression is inherited from earlier processing in a feedforward manner, whereas surround suppression depends on intra-cortical connections.
source: This supports the possible interpretation that cross-orientation suppression is inherited from earlier processing in a feedforward manner, whereas surround suppression depends on intra-cortical connections (either within a cortical area and/or via feedback).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the differences between the two types of suppression.

claim: A large increase in gamma oscillations may reflect locally implemented inhibition, as in surround suppression, but not inherited suppression, as in cross-orientation suppression.
source: A large increase in gamma oscillations may therefore reflect locally implemented inhibition, as in surround suppression, but not inherited suppression, as in cross-orientation suppression.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: The same image properties that are associated with gain control can also be described as signatures of image redundancy or predictability.
source: At a more abstract level, the same image properties that are associated with gain control can also be described as signatures of image redundancy (or predictability).
evidence: This is an alternative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Gamma oscillations can be described as increasing in the presence of image redundancy or predictability.
source: Since gamma oscillations tend to increase in the presence of gain control, they can also be described as increasing in the presence of image redundancy or predictability (Vinck and Bosman, 2016).
evidence: This is an alternative interpretation, supported by a citation.

claim: Early descriptions of center-surround visual receptive fields proposed that surround suppression was part of a coding strategy to compress signals elicited by natural images which contain a lot of redundancy in the form of spatial correlations.
source: In fact, early descriptions of center-surround visual receptive fields proposed that surround suppression was part of a coding strategy to compress signals elicited by natural images which contain a lot of redundancy in the form of spatial correlations (Barlow, 1961).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to early theoretical work.

claim: The circuitry underlying inhibitory mechanisms associated with gamma oscillations are not firmly established.
source: While there is growing evidence that gamma oscillations increase in the presence of gain control or inhibition, the circuitry underlying these inhibitory mechanisms are not firmly established.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Contrast gain control modeled as divisive normalization might be implemented biologically as shunting inhibition.
source: For example, contrast gain control modeled as divisive normalization might be implemented biologically as shunting inhibition (synaptic inhibition which changes the neuronal membrane conductance) (Carandini and Heeger, 1994; Carandini et al., 1997).
evidence: This is a possible biological implementation, supported by citations.

claim: Normalization could be implemented by a circuit that reduces excitation, which in turn also reduces inhibition, as is the case for inhibition-stabilized networks.
source: Alternatively, normalization could be implemented by a circuit that reduces excitation, which in turn also reduces inhibition rather than increases it, as is the case for inhibition-stabilized networks (Ozeki et al., 2009; Tsodyks et al., 1997).
evidence: This is an alternative biological implementation, supported by citations.

claim: In inhibition-stabilized networks, the un-normalized state has a high level of recurrent excitation and inhibition, with the inhibition serving to stabilize the network.
source: In inhibition-stabilized networks, the un-normalized state (e.g., low contrast, no suppressive surround) has a high level of recurrent excitation and inhibition, with the inhibition serving to stabilize the network.
evidence: This describes the properties of inhibition-stabilized networks.

claim: Stimulus manipulations that result in an increase in gain control result in a withdrawal of inhibition in inhibition-stabilized networks.
source: Stimulus manipulations that result in an increase in gain control, such as the addition of a surrounding stimulus or an increase in contrast, paradoxically result in a withdrawal of inhibition.
evidence: This describes the behavior of inhibition-stabilized networks.

claim: Gamma oscillations may be more likely to arise or increase in amplitude in the destabilized state of inhibition-stabilized networks.
source: This, in turn, destabilizes the network, allowing the activity to either die off or explode. Gamma oscillations may be more likely to arise (or to increase in amplitude) in this destabilized state.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of how gamma oscillations might arise in inhibition-stabilized networks.

claim: Large, high-contrast oriented gratings can trigger seizures in patients with photosensitive epilepsy or cause discomfort in healthy subjects.
source: In the extreme, large, high-contrast oriented gratings can even trigger seizures in patients with photosensitive epilepsy or cause discomfort in healthy subjects (Harding et al., 2005; Hermes et al., 2017a; Wilkins et al., 1984).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: A large number of studies have tried to explain the circuit mechanisms that underlie gamma oscillations, including via explicit computational models.
source: A large number of studies have tried to explain the circuit mechanisms that underlie gamma oscillations, including via explicit computational models (Ainsworth et al., 2012; Buzsáki and Wang, 2012; Womelsdorf et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior modeling work.

claim: The Jia et al. (2013) model consists of an excitatory and inhibitory neuron, representing a cortical hypercolumn, with independent inputs and projections, plus a global component representing distributed inputs.
source: This particular model consists of an excitatory and inhibitory neuron, representing a cortical hypercolumn. Each neuron is driven by independent inputs and projects to itself and the other neurons. In addition, a global component is included that represents more distributed inputs, such as horizontal connections or input from higher order visual areas. The global component receives input from the excitatory neurons and sends output to the inhibitory and excitatory neurons.
evidence: This describes the structure of a specific circuit model from prior work.

claim: The Jia et al. (2013) model explains why firing rates and gamma frequency and power can change with different types of inputs.
source: This model explains why firing rates and gamma frequency and power can change with different types of inputs.
evidence: This describes the explanatory power of a specific circuit model from prior work.

claim: The global component in the Jia et al. (2013) model could potentially be driven by long-range horizontal connections between orientation columns in V1 with the same orientation preference.
source: Relating this model to our data, we can potentially imagine the global component being driven by long-range horizontal connections between orientation columns in V1 with the same orientation preference (Angelucci and Bressloff, 2006).
evidence: This is a speculative connection between the circuit model and the current findings, with a citation to prior work on horizontal connections.

claim: None of the circuit models for gamma oscillations operates on visual inputs in the sense of arbitrary pixel intensities.
source: Yet to our knowledge, none of the circuit models for gamma oscillations operates on visual inputs in the sense of arbitrary pixel intensities, as does our image-computable OV model and various models tested recently by Brunet and Fries (2019).
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of circuit models in the field.

claim: The OV model does not describe the neuronal circuitry that produces the oscillations.
source: Our model, however, (as well as those from Brunet and Fries) does not describe the neuronal circuitry that produces the oscillations.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation of the current model.

claim: A more complete understanding of gamma oscillations will likely require a unified account that both generalizes to arbitrary images and also specifies the circuitry that underlies oscillations.
source: A more complete understanding of this intensely studied neural signal will likely require a unified account that both generalizes to arbitrary images and also specifies the circuitry that underlies oscillations.
evidence: This is a statement about future directions for research.

claim: ECoG data were recorded in three subjects who had electrodes implanted for the clinical purpose of epilepsy monitoring.
source: ECoG data were recorded in three subjects (mean age 28, two women) who had electrodes implanted for the clinical purpose of epilepsy monitoring.
evidence: This describes the study participants.

claim: Subjects gave informed consent and the study was approved by the Stanford University IRB and the ethics committee at the University Medical Center Utrecht.
source: Subjects gave informed consent and the study was approved by the Stanford University IRB and the ethics committee at the University Medical Center Utrecht in accordance with the 2013 provisions of the Declaration of Helsinki.
evidence: This describes the ethical approval for the study.

claim: Static visual images were viewed from a distance of ~50 cm and spanned approximately 20 degrees of visual angle.
source: Static visual images were viewed from a distance of ~50 cm and spanned approximately 20 degrees of visual angle.
evidence: This describes the stimulus presentation parameters.

claim: Images were presented for 500 ms (stimulus period), followed by a gray screen for 500 ms (baseline period).
source: Images were presented for 500 ms (stimulus period), followed by a gray screen for 500 ms (baseline period).
evidence: This describes the stimulus presentation timing.

claim: There were 86 different gray scale images that contain spatial frequencies of 3 cycles per degree.
source: There were 86 different gray scale images that contain spatial frequencies of 3 cycles per degree.
evidence: This describes the stimulus set.

claim: Each image was repeated several times (subject 1: 15 times, subject 2: nine times, subject 3: 12 times).
source: Each image was repeated several times (subject 1: 15 times, subject 2: nine times, subject 3: 12 times).
evidence: This describes the experimental design.
